newsitem.title: USA: Widow testifies in Florida assisted suicide trial.
newsitem.headline: Widow testifies in Florida assisted suicide trial.

text.p: The widow of a plaintiff in an assisted suicide lawsuit testified Tuesday that her husband did not want to die but wanted to spare himself and his family the suffering of a lingering death.

Vivienne Cron, testifying on the second day of trial in a lawsuit filed by three terminally ill men against the state of Florida, said her late husband, Robert Cron, watched his mother die of a terminal illness and believed in "death with dignity."
Robert Cron, Chuck Castonguay and Charlie Hall were plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which challenged a 19th Century Florida law that made assisted suicide illegal.

The U.S. Supreme Court Wednesday will hear two hours of arguments in a separate case on whether mentally competent, terminally ill patients have a constitutional right to seek help from their doctors in committing suicide. A ruling is expected by July.

A patient's right to refuse life support, resuscitation efforts or treatment for a fatal disease is widely accepted by courts and ethicists. But advocates of assisted suicide believe a patient should have the right to go a step further and actively decide when to put an end to suffering.
The three Floridians sued the state in February 1996, asking Cecil McIver, a Jupiter physician, be spared from prosecution for helping them end their lives if their pain became intolerable.
Cron, 72, and Castonguay, 65, both died of cancer last year, before the lawsuit could be tried, but were still listed as plaintiffs.

Hall, 35, who contracted AIDS in 1981 through a blood transfusion, testified on the trial's opening day Monday that he wanted to avoid a lingering death and envisioned an assisted suicide in which McIver would prescribe an overdose of drugs for him.

With tears in her eyes, Vivienne Cron, 68, described in Palm Beach Circuit Court her husband's last lucid day, Oct. 20, their 45th wedding anniversary. She said Cron went to bed after eating a couple of bites at the family dinner table. He died three days later.
"He locked out the world. He was going to die," she told the court.
Hall, dressed in white and confined to a wheelchair, sat in the back of the courtroom and listened intently as Cron talked about her husband's death.

Vivienne Cron said she and her husband belonged to the Hemlock Society -- which supports a person's right to commit suicide -- because they were "at an age when they didn't know how it (death) would occur and whether or not they might want help (end it)."

She said her husband knew what terminal illness was like because he had watched his mother die of cancer in 1959. Shortly before her death, the woman had told her son "If I could have gotten up, I would have jumped out the window," Vivienne Cron said.
Lawyers for the state argued Florida had a compelling interest in protecting people, especially the elderly and disabled, who might be coerced into assisted suicide.
Attorney Robert Rivas, representing the plaintiffs, argued Monday that his client, Hall, did not want to die but wanted to be allowed to decide where and when to die.
